1383871,ca.proc.d.1945-10-03.14.1.25,1945-10-03,647c88fa-1673-4147-88b3-b42105bc54e3,ca.m.2918,Mr. CLAXTON:,Minister of National Health and Welfare,OLD AGE PENSIONS,AGE AND INCOME REQUIREMENTS-PROPOSED INCREASE IN AMOUNTS PAYABLE,,There may be some
exceptions over that long period of time, but I think by and large what I have said is true. I would not have mentioned it had it not been for the attitude of the hon. member for Lincoln.

With regard to the special cases he mentioned, I think it is a fact that every one is a matter of provincial administration of laws and regulations which have been agreed to as between the dominion and the provinces. If he has any special cases I wish he would bring them to our attention and we will follow them up. I thought that on two or three points he was completely inaccurate in his interpretation of the law.

It seems to me that a good many of the speakers to-day have been rushing in a crowd to burst through an open door. The discussion has taken place, if I may say so, in a temper which is wholly satisfactory and entirely constructive, but it has to a considerable degree taken place as though the dominion government had never made its proposals to the dominion-provincial conference. Those proposals must be available to hon. members; they have been distributed; and yet it would seem as though those parts which deal with old age pensions have not received very much attention.
I believe hon. members of every party are in agreement that the Old Age Pensions Act as at present in force is not satisfactory. That
Old Age Pensions

is fundamental. In order to do something about it the federal government took the only course possible, namely, to put before the provinces proposals that the present act should be changed. Those proposals will be found at page 37 and following of the dominion government's proposals to the dominion-provincial conference. There will be found a review of the legislation as it exists, some references to legislation in other countries, and then the dominion government's proposals, first, for a national old age pension at age seventy of $30 a month without a means test; and second, for old age assistance to people between sixty-five and sixty-nine years of $30 a month with a means test, to be provincially administered and to be contributed to on an equal basis by the dominion and provincial governments. These two proposals are elaborated there; and the hon. member for Spadina quoted from the proposals the reasons and objects of the federal government in putting them forward.

These proposals have been put before the provinces. They were put before them at the conference which began on August 6, and formed part of a comprehensive body of proposals to deal with post-war reconstruction and the social security of Canada. They were not put forward in isolation; they were the result of years of study and they were comprehensive. Furthermore, they were part of a plan which we are convinced will work, and which is the only plan so far put before the people of Canada of such a nature or of any nature to cover the whole field of employment, reconversion and social security, as well as finance.

When the proposals were put before the provinces they received what I think anyone who was present would regard as a sympathetic reception. Certainly the provinces gave every assurance that the proposals would receive serious consideration, and we in this house can only take it to be the case that they are receiving serious consideration to-day. With that as the situation confronting us at this moment, it seems to me it would be quite inappropriate for this government to make some totally different proposal with regard to anything of a major nature here. The place where we can do it is before the conference and the time to do it is at the conference.

That is not just a technical objection. It is a very serious objection because of this. The plan suggested by several speakers in the debate on the address, and suggested in the speech to-day by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), was for old age pensions to be paid to all citizens on attaining the age of sixty years, at $50 a month without a

means test. The estimate which the Dominion Bureau of Statistics has given me would indicate that in the year 1948, $50 a month to every person of sixty years of age and over would cost the federal government $850 million for that year alone. When I tell the house that the total amount raised by personal income tax for the year 1944-1945 is estimated to be 672 million hon. members will see something of the magnitude of the proposal put forward by the hon. member.

In other words, the cost of this proposal would be more than the total personal income tax paid by the Canadian people during the last year. That has a definite bearing on our relations with the provinces. We have with them an agreement under which we have agreed to retire from tax fields by an amount sufficient to enable them to raise certain sums in income taxation. Were we to impose taxes or keep in force taxes of the nature required by my hon. friend's proposals, we could not carry out our undertaking with the provinces.
This proposal is being put forward, too, at a time when I think the great body of the Canadian people would like to see a reduction in income taxation.

,Liberal,,Brooke Claxton,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=647c88fa-1673-4147-88b3-b42105bc54e3&Language=E&Section=ALL

old folks.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Joseph William Burton,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=c39f4538-336c-4b45-8010-93f1bec0c06f&Language=E&Section=ALL
1383873,ca.proc.d.1945-10-03.14.1.27,1945-10-03,647c88fa-1673-4147-88b3-b42105bc54e3,ca.m.2918,Mr. CLAXTON:,Minister of National Health and Welfare,OLD AGE PENSIONS,AGE AND INCOME REQUIREMENTS-PROPOSED INCREASE IN AMOUNTS PAYABLE,,That reduction in taxation can be made, and we believe it can be made at the same time as the social security legislation of Canada is put on a footing second to none in the -whole civilized world. We believe that can be done and will be done if these proposals are put into effect. But we cannot do that if at the same time we put on our people a burden of taxation which crushes all initiative and which prevents all enterprise from carrying on successfully at a profit. Whether enterprise is carried on publicly or privately, it can make or lose money. It does not make much difference whether it is done publicly or privately from that point of view. But there is the other element. Hon. members and the people of Canada are looking to a great amount of trade after the war as one of the important factors by which we can maintain the very high standard of living we have achieved. We shall not have that trade unless we are in a position to meet prices, and that cannot be done if we have taxation on a scale such as would be required here.

What we have done in our proposals is not to take old age pensions just by themselves and say we will spend S850 million and give old age pensions at the age of sixty years to a lot of people who will not need them anyway. What we have done is to look over the whole economy of Canada and study the
Old Age Pensions

situation of the people of Canada in relation to their needs, and we have tried to put together a balanced programme of social security, having regard not only to old age, not only to the provision of assistance for our children, but also to health, unemployment and preventive medicine.

These proposals, which hon. members will find in the green book, have been worked out so as to present a balance, and we believe that * the provision of $200 million for old age pensions, payable without proof of need, to everyone at seventy years of age, at the rate of $30 a month, is well within possibilities. We believe that the provision of health insurance, which may cost $150 million to the federal government, is well within possibilities. And these measures, taken with family allowances, which may cost $200 million net, will present to the Canadian people a body of social legislation which, taken with that already in force in the provinces, or under consideration in the provinces, will put Canada in the forefront of the world to-day in the field of social security legislation.

One word in conclusion. A good deal has been said about the old age provisions in other countries. I say to my hon. friends that if the old age pension put before the provinces in the dominion proposals is carried into effect we shall have within Canada the most generous old age pension system anywhere in the world, and I calculate that by dividing the amount of the cost by the number of possible recipients. I say similarly, if my hon. friends will total up the anticipated costs of the social security legislation put forward in these proposals, and add to them the costs of the social security legislation already in force in the provinces and in the dominion, they will see that Canada will be leading the world in its per capita contribution to the welfare of the Canadian people if the present plans are accepted by the provinces and by this house.

As I say, this represents a comprehensive plan. It would not do at this moment to pick out this and change that, and it would not be keeping faith with the provinces. We have put before them in all seriousness and sincerity these proposals; we are willing to carry them out just as soon as they can be agreed to, and we hope they will be carried out. We believe, too, that the surest way of securing what my hon. friends would want would be that they should assist us in presenting these proposals to the people of Canada and to the provinces, so that they will secure the support which we believe they deserve.
